posts.title: 25 year hidden find
posts.text: Welcome, and what a find! A tub that's been in a loft for 25 years can be a real treasure chest, so taking your time is exactly the right approach. A few things that have helped me with lots like this: 1. Start with the instructions. Each booklet has the set number on it, so make a list of those first. Then look each one up on BrickLink or Rebrickable to get the full parts inventory, which tells you exactly what to look for and what's missing. 2. Sort roughly before you build. Separating by colour (or by type: plates, bricks, slopes, Technic) makes finding pieces much quicker than rummaging through the whole tub for every step. 3. Minifigures: put them to one side and keep them safe. You can identify them in the BrickLink catalogue by theme and year. Figures from around 2000 can be worth more than people expect, especially if they're complete with their original accessories. 4. Pricing: the BrickLink price guide is the most reliable. Look at the "last 6 months sales" for used items rather than current asking prices. A complete set with instructions is usually worth much more than the same pieces sold loose, so it's worth finishing sets before you decide what to sell. 5. Cleaning: warm (not hot) water and a little washing-up liquid works well, but keep anything with stickers or electrics out of the water and let everything dry fully before storing. Good luck, and enjoy it!

posts.title: KineBrick: LEGO Technic models that move in the browser, worked out from the parts
posts.text: KineBrick is a web viewer that makes LDraw models move the way they are designed. Drag a part: push a car and it rolls, turn its steering wheel and the front wheels steer, ctrl-click a tire and the car and drivetrain move. Nothing is animated by hand. It finds each part’s connection points (from LDCad’s shadow library), works out how the parts connect, and solves the mechanism in realtime. Try it: https://erik-larsen.github.io/kinebrick/ Source (MIT): https://github.com/erik-larsen/kinebrick What works: gear trains, bevel gears, differentials, worms, gearboxes, steering, cranks and pistons, linkages, racks, chains and tracks, winch strings, and collisions. You can also drop in your own .ldr or .mpd file (though expect there to be many bugs still). It’s a work in progress. I’m going through the OMR’s Technic sets, oldest first, and 1977–1980 are mostly done. I checked all 185 OMR Technic sets against the functions in their instruction books: 37% of functions work, 32% partly work, 17% don’t, and 14% aren’t checked yet. Only about 12 sets have every function working. There are no forces yet, so springs, shocks, pneumatics, etc. wait for version 2.0. I welcome any feedback, especially about a mechanism that moves wrong (for the built-in models, copy the page address, since it keeps the model and its settings), or a set you’d like to see working next. Built on LDraw, LDCad’s shadow library, LSynth and three.js. Many thanks to everyone behind them.

posts.title: Using Claude AI for new ports and translations
posts.text: Newer version add tc controller emulation, vitual optocoupler disks, two interfaces control, support for bricklogo and tc connect, support for power functions via bricklogo. https://htmlhoster.com/p/JE0384NC/ Claude wrote: "I've added an emulation of the missing LEGO TC Controller to the editor (Version 18). The book shows it was software, not a separate box. It was a resident program called CONTROL.EXE, with a keyboard "direct control" window and a Turbo Pascal unit called LTCC. I rebuilt both from the book's descriptions, so the details are not guaranteed to match the original. I tested it with scripted keystrokes and a simulated serial device, not a real Interface A. The new code is in the page, the Pascal editor mode and the Interface A panel. Direct control: a new "Direct control" button opens a window in the Interface A panel, styled after the book's figure 7.3. The keys follow the book: Keys 0–5 toggle outputs. The arrow keys drive motors A and B, and PgUp/PgDn drive C. Space switches everything off. Shift-right plus a key raises a power level, 0–8, and Shift-left lowers it. Counters A and B reset with the 6 and 7 keys, and Esc closes the window. Every button also works by click. A "last instruction" line shows the Pascal command that matches what you pressed. LTCC unit: in the Pascal mode, uses LTCC; now gives you the unit's full procedure list: BitOn, Motor, SetPower, the flash, counter, clock and timer calls, Wait and ResetController. Without that line you get the same "Unknown identifier" error as in Turbo Pascal. There are five new examples: a running light power levels frequency and counters flash and timer counting turns Power levels: with the real Interface A connected, levels 1–7 are produced by pulsing the outputs. I tested that against the simulated serial device only. Level 4 gave half on and half off. Counters in simulation: a "Virtual count disc" checkbox, on by default, makes a simulated disc on motors A and B feed inputs 6 and 7. I calibrated it so the frequency example gives 142 Hz, as in the book. The counter reading was 573 against the book's 564. The Direct procedure only prints a note during a simulated run, because the window can't take over a running program. The motor mode names in the book are only partly legible, so I accept lft, rgt, trn and hlt, plus the English words left, right, toggle and halt. Should I add a second interface at address 926 next? The book says the card can be jumpered to it, and the TC Controller had a matching second-interface variant (CONTROL2 and LTCC2, opened with Alt-J)."

posts.title: [WIP] Jamestown: A Colonial Redcoat Capital
posts.text: Jamestown Here is a project I’ve slowly been piecing together for over a year now with some contribution from my son. Jamestown is a highly fictionalized version of the first permanent English colony in North America, (not surprisingly) named Jamestown. The actual Jamestown was established in 1607 but eventually faded away in favor of nearby Williamsburg, which became the capital of Virginia in 1699. Both are located about an hour away from where I live. This display is based off a combination of both Jamestown and Williamsburg and geographically set in that general area. If one is predisposed to locations closer to “big water” this display can easily be imagined as an early version of Norfolk, Virginia. The display itself is baseplate based. It’s 3x3 32x32 stud baseplates for a total of nine plates. Five of these are green and four are blue. The design is simple. It is not meant to be as detailed and elaborate as some of the MOCs I’ve seen posted here. With that said, I do intend to keep evolving it, adding details to the buildings (inside and out). I don’t want it to become too elaborate though. It’s supposed to fit right in with the vintage Imperial Redcoats I love so much. And by extension the vintage pirates theme overall. With this in mind, the sand is “bright yellow” and the water is the basic blue of those old baseplates. I always felt like the one thing the theme was missing was civilians just living their lives. The Islanders sort of addressed this, but there still were no imperial civilians. Jamestown is my biggest attempt to address that gap. This post about Jamestown is also the first out of several I will share intended to weave my own lore into the actual displays I’ve built. It’s amazing to me how combining sets can lead to imaginative storytelling, even for a grown adult who never fully outgrew his love for vintage Lego pirates! With that in mind it was important to me to integrate some of the original vintage sets into it. I didn’t use any software applications to design this display; I just studied a few pics of what early 18th century waterfront communities may have looked like and tried to match what I saw. I do love these new “brick” bricks, which weren’t available when the original waves were introduced. I think even in a simple design like this they really do give it some good texture. I also made sure to do some buildings in plain white brick, again to help “phase” the overall aesthetic with the vintage stuff. When we first started building, my son and I went back and forth between naming it Jamestown or Williamsburg, which eventually emerged as the colonial capital of Virginia. We decided on Jamestown for a few reasons. One, it’s a riverfront display, and Jamestown was built on the banks of the James River while Williamsburg is inland a couple miles. We also just like the historic Jamestown site quite a bit more than Colonial Williamsburg. Truthfully, if you are on this forum and your interest in Lego Pirates can be even loosely tied to the Age of Sail, North American and Caribbean colonial history, and the people who lived in these eras, you can’t go wrong with either location. With my Lego displays I’m not a stickler for historical accuracy. I’ll place my displays somewhere between 1715 and 1725. In this reimagined Jamestown, the original site was not phased out but grew into a colonial city that exerted its influence on the entire hemisphere. posts.title: Wet Winds - an RC windmill building operation
posts.text: Together with the talented Appie we entertained the visitors of Legoworld Utrecht with a windmill building operation this year. The goal is to set up a windmill completely remotely controlled, without any manual help. This is done with massive crane barges, pulled along with tugboats. The parts for the windmills are supplied on separate barges. The building operation runs on two Powered Up hubs each, one for the tugboat and one for the crane. The windmills use Power Functions. Brickcontroller2 and Pybricks were used to control the MOCs. Even though the windmill designs and construction are radically different, we found that construction time per windmill was remarkably similar. Maybe a fun challenge for others to try? We're convinced there are way more possibilities for other designs.
